seo.title: Karmic tail 18 6 15 compatibility: The Moon, The Lovers, The Devil
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 6 15 compatibility: a couple meets through an image of each other, learns to choose the living person and to stop holding on to “mine”.

title: Karmic tail 18-6-15 in compatibility: a couple and its phantom
short: For ten years Greeks and Trojans fought over Helen, and yet, if Stesichorus, Herodotus and Euripides are to be believed, she was never in Troy. In Euripides, Paris carried off a phantom woven out of air. The karmic tail 18-6-15 in compatibility tells the same story about a couple. Two people come together through an image of each other (The Moon), they have to recognise and choose the living person (The Lovers), and the main task is to stop serving the image and holding on to the thought “you are mine” (The Devil).

paragraphs: The first to tell this story was the poet Stesichorus, who lived at the turn of the seventh and sixth centuries BC. At first, like everyone else, he sang of Helen the runaway, the woman who started the war. According to the legend Plato retells in the Phaedrus, the poet was struck blind for it. Plato names his fault precisely — κακηγορία, evil-speaking. Stesichorus understood the cause and composed a palinode, a song of recantation: “That saying is not true; thou didst not go within the well-oared ships, nor didst thou come to the walls of Troy” (trans. H. N. Fowler). As soon as he finished it, he could see again.

In the second book of his Histories (chapters 112–120) Herodotus wrote down what the Egyptian priests told him. A storm drove Paris's ship to Egypt, King Proteus kept Helen with him, and she spent the whole war there. The Trojans honestly told the Greeks that Helen was not in their city, but the Greeks would not believe them, “although they spoke the truth” (trans. A. D. Godley). Herodotus adds that Homer, in his opinion, knew this version but rejected it because it suited epic poetry less well.

In 412 BC Euripides turned this into a tragedy, Helen. Hera, offended by the judgement of Paris, gave him not Helen but “a phantom endowed with life, that she made in my image out of the breath of heaven”, as E. P. Coleridge translates it. In the prologue Helen says: “Paris thought that I was his, although I never was — an idle fancy!” The Greek line is shorter and harder: καὶ δοκεῖ μ᾽ ἔχειν — κενὴν δόκησιν, οὐκ ἔχων, “and he thinks he has me — an empty seeming, not having me” (our translation). And the prize of the war was a name: “yet not I, but my name alone”.

Waite's divinatory list for The Moon reads: “Hidden enemies, danger, calumny, darkness, terror, deception, occult forces, error.” It is almost a table of contents for the myth. The hidden enemy is Hera. The calumny is Stesichorus's evil-speaking and the phantom's own last words about Helen, who “hath borne an evil name without reason”. The deception is the substitution. The error is a ten-year war over a cloud. For Waite, The Moon is “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”, a light that only reflects. Euripides' phantom is exactly that kind of light: a reflection that walks, speaks and is embraced.

sections.h2: One word at both ends of the tail
paragraphs: In Euripides, Helen's phantom is called εἴδωλον. The word comes from the verb “to see”, and it means an image, a reflection in water or a mirror, a shade, a ghost. A century and a half to two centuries later the translators of the Bible into Greek took the same word. In the book of Exodus (20:4) the commandment reads: οὐ ποιήσεις σεαυτῷ εἴδωλον οὐδὲ παντὸς ὁμοίωμα ὅσα ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἄνω. In Brenton's English Septuagint: “Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor likeness of anything, whatever things are in the heaven above.”

Put Euripides' prologue next to it. Hera “made like me” (ὁμοιώσασα) a “phantom” (εἴδωλον) composed “of heaven” (οὐρανοῦ). The same three ideas as the commandment, from the same Greek roots: idol, likeness, heaven. The translators of the Torah were of course not quoting a tragedian. All the more striking, then, that the language itself linked them: in Greek “phantom” and “idol” are one word, and the English word idol comes from it.

For Benebell Wen, “the theme of The Devil is the worship of false idols.” Waite says of The Moon: “The intellectual light is a reflection.” The tail 18-6-15 begins with the eidolon as reflection and ends with the eidolon as idol. Between them stand The Lovers — the only one of the three cards where, in Waite, two people stand “unveiled before each other”. That is the hidden plot of the tail: the image with which the couple began will either become a living person or become an idol to be served. This link through the Greek word is our own reading; neither Waite nor Wen draws it.

A similar link, without any cards, was drawn by Plato. In book nine of the Republic (586b–c) he speaks of pleasures mixed with pain: they are “phantoms of true pleasure”, they “beget mad loves of themselves in senseless souls”, and they are “fought for, as Stesichorus says the wraith of Helen was fought for at Troy through ignorance of the truth” (trans. Paul Shorey). Just before this he describes people who, like cattle, kick and butt one another “with horns and hooves of iron” in their insatiable greed for such pleasures. For Plato, Helen's phantom is no longer a myth but a name for passion for a likeness. It is very close to the passage from The Moon to The Devil written into this tail.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a common language of guesses
paragraphs: The entry to the task shows what the couple wants together, what common language it speaks and what it agrees on. The Moon in this place wants mystery. Not a dull “how was your day”, but a world only the two of them understand: half-hints, games, night-time talks, the feeling that the other sees what nobody else sees. In its plus, Lisovskaya describes The Moon in a couple as intuition, respect for personal space and the habit of discovering something new in the partner every year.

Wen makes an observation about The Moon that takes the blame off this entry: “the first light of the divine, the first clarity to be offered,” may come “from the moon, the reflection, rather than from the sun itself.” Two people really do see each other first by reflected light — in the light of their own hopes. That is not a mistake; it is a way in. In Richard Strauss and Hugo von Hofmannsthal's Die ägyptische Helena (The Egyptian Helen, first performed on 6 June 1928 in Dresden), Menelaus raises a dagger over his wife, but the lights in the hall go down, only moonlight falls inside, a beam lands on Helen's face, and the hand with the dagger drops. The stage direction says he stands as if spellbound by her beauty. At the entry The Moon saves: the image stops the blow.
But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The common language of guesses quietly becomes a language of assumptions:

ul: He is silent at dinner, she already knows why, and she spends the evening arguing not with him but with her version of him.
One of them keeps the image of “who you were that first summer” and measures the present person against it, and the present person never quite measures up.
The couple has a lovely legend for friends — “we understood each other at first sight” — and everything that does not fit it gets hidden: tiredness, boredom, disagreement.
One of them plays the role they were loved for, and a year later the role irritates them both.

paragraphs: Among the couple's tasks in the minus of The Moon, Lisovskaya names exactly this: a false image created at the start that later collapses, jealousy and resentment born of invented stories, adapting to the partner in a way that ends in irritation. Euripides shows the mechanism in a single exchange. Menelaus, seeing his living wife, calls on the night goddess of the crossroads: “O Hecate, giver of light, send thy visions favourably!” Helen replies: “In me thou beholdest no spectre of the night, attendant on the queen of phantoms.” Someone who has lived a long time with an image sees a ghost in a living person. Helen's answer is the best advice for this entry: check things by daylight.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: “the greatness of my troubles convinces me”
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the wish to the main task. In Waite, The Lovers is “the card of human love”; in Wen, it is “partnership with one other person” and a choice with a moral price. In this tail the choice is very concrete: whom to believe — the image or the person.

Euripides' recognition scene reads like the minutes of such a choice. Menelaus pushes his wife away: “Nor yet am I in my single person the husband of two wives.” The other one, he explains, is “the inmate of yonder cave, whom I from Troy convey”. Then he looks closer and admits: “Thy form resembles her, but the real truth robs me of this belief.” Helen: “Who then shall teach thee, unless it be thine own eyes?” And finally the key line: “The greatness of my troubles at Troy convinces me; thou dost not.” The Greek is just as blunt: “the greatness of my toils there persuades me, not you” (our literal translation).

This is why people hold on to an image: it has been paid for. Ten years of war and seven years of wandering would turn into nonsense if the woman in the cave were a phantom. Menelaus believes not his eyes but the price. In a couple this sounds familiar: “I have put so much into this”, “I have put up with so much for this person” — and what has been invested gets in the way of seeing who is actually standing there.

In Euripides the resolution is simple. A messenger runs in: the cave is empty, the phantom has risen into the sky. As it left, it told the truth: they all died “in the false belief that Helen was in the hands of Paris”. Only after that comes the embrace. The image did not have to be smashed: it left by itself, having “stayed my appointed time”. For a couple like this, the middle of the task is a series of small recognitions. The strong one turns out to be lost, the light one vulnerable, the mysterious one simply tired. Each time it is possible to resent the person for not matching the image, and each time it is possible to choose them again.

Among the tasks of The Lovers, Lisovskaya names idealisation and perfectionism in the relationship, the insecurity from which jealousy and control grow, and self-love inside the couple, which one partner sometimes teaches the other. In its plus the same card brings sincerity, no secrets and shared decisions even in small things. For this tail the plus of The Lovers is the ability to say: I see you not as I imagined you, and I choose you as you are.

sections.h2: Main task: “he thinks he has me”
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mostly through its minus. For The Devil in a couple, Lisovskaya lists control and pursuit, jealousy and the wish to own, attempts to hold the partner through intimacy, a child, money or status, obsession with a person, silence about one's own desires, and a union that drags both down. Her closing thought on the fifteenth energy is that nobody belongs to anybody.

Euripides builds the play on the verb ἔχειν — “to have, to hold”. Paris “thought that I was his, although I never was”. The phantom tells the Greeks they died believing Paris had Helen, whom he never had. Menelaus explains why he cannot believe his wife: “Herein is my dilemma; I have another wife” — and again the Greek word is ἔχω. The whole play is about people sure they hold what they do not have. Here is the Devil of this couple in one image: a cave on the shore where sailors guard a likeness of a wife, and a husband who calls it “mine”.
In everyday life the cave looks ordinary:

ul: “Mine” turns into rights: to know passwords, to approve friends, to decide what the partner wears — all in the name of the image: “that's not like you”.
Sacrifices turn into a bill. Menelaus's “greatness of my troubles” becomes “I gave things up for you”, “I wasted my best years on you”. The bill holds both of them tighter than any chain.
The couple is held together by a shared mortgage and a shared legend, and both are afraid to admit that the legend stopped being about them long ago.
Each guards the image of “the good partner” and so keeps quiet about what they really want. Desire goes underground and comes back out as resentment.

paragraphs: There are always two in the cave: the one who is guarded and the one who guards. Neither is free. In the myth the husband holds the image, but in a real couple the roles are not handed out by gender: either partner can hold on to the image and to “mine”, and more often both do, by turns.

The Devil has a plus too, and for this tail it matters most. Lisovskaya describes it as attachment in the good sense: the partners accept each other's dark sides, forgive mistakes, talk openly about desires, and there is a lot of passion and readiness to change for love. A couple with 18-6-15 reaches this plus not when it gets rid of the mystery, but when it stops guarding it.

If control in a couple has already turned into threats, surveillance or violence, this is not a “karmic task” to be sat out to the end. In danger, call a local emergency number; for support, turn to a psychologist or a crisis line.

sections.h2: Two cups: Hofmannsthal turns Euripides inside out
paragraphs: Two thousand three hundred years after Euripides, Hofmannsthal wrote his own Helen for Strauss and turned the myth inside out. In The Egyptian Helen the phantom is no longer the truth but a merciful lie. The sorceress Aithra gives Menelaus lotus, the drink of forgetting, and tells him that when Paris reached for his wife, the gods secretly looked after the husband and laid in the abductor's arms “an airy image, a fragrant ghost, the kind they fool mortal men with” (ein Luftgebild, ein duftig Gespenst — our translation). And the real Helen, she claims, slept all those years in a castle on the slopes of the Atlas. “Drink with me!” says Aithra, and the stage direction specifies that she herself only pretends to drink.

The drug of forgetting is old in this couple's story. Already in book four of the Odyssey, Helen, back home in Sparta, casts into the wine a drug she received from the Egyptian woman Polydamna, “a drug to quiet all pain and strife, and bring forgetfulness of every ill” (trans. A. T. Murray). Hofmannsthal said what Homer left unsaid: at what price.

The lotus worked, and Helen saw what it had done to her. Her husband now takes her “for a strange woman you brought him in the night, and thinks that with me he has betrayed the Helen he believes dead” (Er kennt mich für ein fremdes Weib… — our translation). The image of the “pure” wife has made the living wife a stranger and the husband an adulterer: unfaithful to her, with her. The loop of The Moon and The Devil could not be drawn more sharply.

Aithra's casket holds two flasks. The second is remembrance, “the drink of hell” from which, she says, even the blessed gods flee. Helen seizes exactly that one: “This is the drink I need! Remembrance!” Aithra warns her: let it touch your lips and you will become a living dead woman. Helen answers that it was the first potion that made her dead while alive, that very night.

The couple's final exchange could stand as an epigraph to this tail. Helen asks: “Do you belong so wholly to her?” Menelaus answers: “Hast du mich jemals besessen? Laß mich der Toten und lebe!” — “Did you ever possess me? Leave me to the dead woman, and live!” (our translation). The German besessen here means “possessed” in the sense of owned, but the same word also means “possessed” as in obsessed. Menelaus thinks the cup holds poison and will not let his wife drink. Helen raises the cup to her lips: “You drink it to the other one — I drink with you!” Almost the same words Aithra said for show, Helen says in earnest, and she drinks first.

Menelaus drinks remembrance and sees his wife anew: “I see you as no mortal man has ever yet seen his wife!” And then: “Faithless one, ever the one, ever new!” (Ungetreue, ewig eine, ewig neue — our translation). He stops splitting her into the woman who was at Troy and the woman he loves: the libretto says the two are now united into one. This is the way out of The Devil into its plus: to accept the partner's dark side instead of guarding a likeness of them. And at the same time it is a return to The Lovers, where two people stand unveiled before each other.

Hofmannsthal does not preach forgiving everything. He shows that peace bought with forgetting rests on a substitution. For a couple with tail 18-6-15 this is the main temptation: to agree not to remember, to edit each other's past into a beautiful image and live with the image. The way out is to remember together.

sections.h2: The empty tomb: how a couple leaves the cave
paragraphs: In Euripides one word recurs at three key moments — κενός, “empty”. The empty seeming of possession in the prologue. The empty bed that Menelaus is ready to carry off instead of his wife — in Coleridge's version: “What! wilt leave me, and take that phantom bride away?” And the empty tomb through which the couple escapes.

The plan is Helen's: “Dost thou consent to be dead in word, though not really so?” Menelaus agrees — “I am ready to be dead in word, though not in deed” — but grumbles that “there is something stale about this story” (our translation). Helen asks the king of Egypt for a ship so that she can bury her drowned husband at sea, in an empty tomb. On that ship the two of them sail away together.

To leave the cave, what gets buried is not a person but a role: the Menelaus who fought ten years over a cloud. They do it together, by a shared plan, and here The Lovers work as an alliance. For a couple with this tail the story yields several practices:

ul: **Palinode.** Stesichorus regained his sight when he took back his evil-speaking. Now and then a couple can take back an old story about the partner, out loud: “For years I said you always ruin everything. It isn't true.” In the Phaedrus, Socrates uncovers his head before speaking his own palinode about love: he gave his first speech with his head covered for shame.
**The daylight check.** Telling “I know” from “I imagine”. Asking rather than guessing, especially late in the evening, when The Moon writes the scripts.
**Price is not proof.** Noticing the moment when “I have put so much in” replaces “I see”.
**Drink with, not to.** Remembering the hard chapters together, without turning the partner into either a stranger or a saint.
**Desires out loud.** The Devil grows where desires are kept silent. In its plus it is precisely about talking about them openly.
**“Mine” is not a right.** Friends, time alone and private messages stay with each person. Closeness that runs on permissions is a cave, not a home.

paragraphs: The tail 18-6-15 occurs in roughly one couple in 143 (0.697%) and ranks 49th of the 97 couple tails — right in the middle of the list, neither rare nor ordinary.

It is formed by only four combinations of the partners' personal tails. In 86% of such couples they are 12-16-4 and 6-17-11, in 9% 15-20-5 and 3-13-10, in 3% 12-19-7 and 6-14-8, in 2% 9-15-6 and 9-18-9. Hence the main clue: in 89% of such couples neither partner has either The Moon or The Devil in their personal tail. Someone brings their own Moon in only 2% of couples, their own Devil in 11%. The image and the tether of this tail are almost always born between two people rather than brought in by one of them. As in Euripides: Hera made the phantom “out of the breath of heaven”, and it belonged to neither spouse.

There is an arithmetical detail too. In each of the four combinations the middles of the personal tails add up to exactly 33: 16 + 17, 20 + 13, 19 + 14, 15 + 18. The couple's middle six always comes from one and the same sum.

The centre of the chart in such couples is “The atmosphere inside the couple”, what happens between two people when nobody is watching. In 81.8% it holds 21, The World, in 18.2% 3, The Empress. The World never appears in the centre of a personal chart for any date of birth: this card in the centre exists only for a couple. In Lisovskaya, The World in a couple's atmosphere means, in its plus, full acceptance of the partner even in their minus, and in its minus, re-educating the partner to suit oneself and illusions about the relationship. It is the same fork as in the tail: accept the living person or remake them to fit the image.

“The couple's values” hold 9, The Hermit, in 75.5% of cases and 18, The Moon, in 24.5%. Of the Hermit's lantern Waite writes: “It is a star which shines in the lantern.” A light of one's own instead of a reflected one is not a bad value for a couple that began with a reflection. And in every fourth such couple The Moon stands both at the entry and among the values: mystery is itself a value for them, and the task is not to kill it but to stop worshipping it.

Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal charts, reduced to 22. The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it too is the sum of the partners' middles.

First partner, 14.04.1975: day 14, month 4, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task 14 + 4 + 22 = 40 → 4, centre 14 + 4 + 22 + 4 = 44 → 8, entry to the task 4 + 8 = 12, middle 4 + 12 = 16. Personal tail: 12-16-4.
Second partner, 05.11.1975: day 5, month 11, year 22. Main task 5 + 11 + 22 = 38 → 11, centre 5 + 11 + 22 + 11 = 49 → 13, entry 11 + 13 = 24 → 6, middle 11 + 6 = 17. Personal tail: 6-17-11.

This is the most common combination, accounting for 86% of such couples. This couple's centre is 8 + 13 = 21, The World, and “The couple's values” are 9, The Hermit. And on the point “What to create together” (the month, 4 + 11) stands another Devil, 15. Lisovskaya reads this point only in its plus and writes that fifteen there very often means a way out of dependence. In this couple The Devil is both the task and what they are to create together: a union where attachment does not turn into a tether.

The same numbers form the couple tail 18-15-6. It occurs in 0.476% of couples, and its centre is always 12, The Hanged Man. The order changes the meaning: there The Devil stands in the middle and The Lovers are the main task. A couple with 18-15-6 goes through the tether in order to learn to choose. A couple with 18-6-15 goes through the choice in order to learn not to hold on.
There is also a personal karmic tail 18-6-15 — one person's, from a date of birth. It is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article about it.

ul: Euripides, Helen (412 BC): translation by E. P. Coleridge (1891); Greek text from the Perseus edition; where marked, our translation.
Plato, Phaedrus, 243a–b: the story of Stesichorus and his palinode (trans. H. N. Fowler); Republic, IX, 586b–c: “phantoms of true pleasure” (trans. Paul Shorey).
Herodotus, Histories, book II, 112–120: the Egyptian priests' account of Helen at the court of Proteus (trans. A. D. Godley).
Homer, Odyssey, IV, 220–221: Helen's drug against “all pain and strife” (trans. A. T. Murray).
The Septuagint, Exodus 20:4, in the Greek and in Brenton's English translation.
H. von Hofmannsthal and R. Strauss, Die ägyptische Helena (The Egyptian Helen, 1928): libretto; translations of quotations are ours.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922): The Moon, The Lovers, The Hermit.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Moon, The Lovers, The Devil.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple's points and energies 6, 9, 15, 18 and 21 in a couple.

**Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** What the couple wants together: mystery, depth, being understood without words. This wish is how the couple enters the task, and it is also what resists: a shared language of guesses easily turns into a language of assumptions.

**Middle of the task — 6, The Lovers.** What the couple goes through: recognition and choice. Sooner or later they have to decide whom to believe — the image they have paid so much for, or the person standing next to them.
**Main task — 15, The Devil.** The couple's main trial, read through its minus: attachment to an image, the wish to own, control. What has to be learned is that nobody belongs to anybody.

intro: A couple's tail does not predict what will happen to two people. It shows where their union most often stumbles and where it keeps its reserves of strength. What follows is the evidence: in a Greek tragedy, in one Greek word, in an opera of 1928 and in the numbers themselves.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 18-6-15 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's chart: entry to the task 18 (The Moon), middle 6 (The Lovers), main task 15 (The Devil). The couple comes together through an image of each other, goes through recognising and choosing the living person, and its main trial is attachment to the image and the wish to own the partner.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail shows tasks, not a verdict. The Devil as the main task is read through its minus — control, jealousy, living for an image — but in its plus it is passion, acceptance of each other's dark sides and open talk about desires. This method gives no compatibility percentages.

faq.q: Who in the couple holds the image, and who carries it?
faq.a: The cards do not hand out roles by gender or character and do not assign blame. In the myth it is Menelaus who holds the image, but in a real couple it can be either partner, and more often both, by turns.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 18-6-15 different from a personal tail 18-6-15?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date of birth, and its points have their own roles. A couple's tail is formed from two personal charts: each point is the sum of the partners' points. Texts about one do not carry over to the other.

faq.q: How do you calculate the couple's tail 18-6-15?
faq.a: Calculate the two personal charts and add up the matching points of the tail: the entries, the middles and the main tasks, reducing sums above 22. For example, 14.04.1975 (tail 12-16-4) and 05.11.1975 (tail 6-17-11) give 18-6-15. The middle is not recalculated from the couple's outer numbers.

The roles are not handed out by gender: either partner can hold on to the image, and more often both do, by turns. If control has already turned into threats, surveillance or violence, this is not a task to be sat out: in danger, call a local emergency number; for support, turn to a psychologist or a crisis line.

The Devil has a plus too: accepting each other's dark sides, forgiving mistakes, talking openly about desires. **A couple with 18-6-15 reaches it not when it gets rid of the mystery, but when it stops guarding it.**

In 1928 Hofmannsthal and Strauss turned the myth inside out in the opera The Egyptian Helen. There the phantom is a merciful lie: a sorceress gives Menelaus the lotus of forgetting and assures him that only “an airy image” was at Troy, while the real Helen slept all those years. The lotus worked, and the husband began to take his wife for a strange woman with whom he was betraying the “pure” Helen. The image made the living wife a stranger. So Helen herself chooses the second flask — the drink of remembrance. Menelaus asks: “Did you ever possess me?” She raises the cup to her lips: “You drink it to the other one — I drink with you!” Having drunk remembrance, he sees her anew: “Faithless one, ever the one, ever new!” **Peace bought with forgetting rests on a substitution; the way out is to remember together.**

In Euripides the couple escapes through an empty tomb: Menelaus agrees to be “dead in word, though not in deed”, and the two of them sail away on a ship begged for a funeral. What gets buried is not a person but a role — the man who fought ten years over a cloud. Several practices follow from this. Now and then, take back an old story about the partner out loud, like the poet Stesichorus, who by legend regained his sight when he recanted his slander of Helen. Tell “I know” from “I imagine”, and ask rather than guess. Notice when “I have put so much in” replaces “I see”. And remember that “mine” is not a right: friends, time alone and private messages stay with each person.

captions.M: To want mystery and a world only the two of you share
captions.N: To choose the living person, not the image
captions.D: To stop guarding the image and clinging to “mine”

unit.meaning: Your task is to choose each other as living people, not images, and to remember that “mine” is not a right.
